summary: A proposal from the BBN authors, following an FTP meeting, for letting a user program connect two servers so a file moves directly from one to the other. It proposes a PASV command to make a server listen for the connection, along with the SOCK command. It continues RFC 438.

eli5.summary: Two houses need to swap a parcel, so a helper tells one to wait at the door and the other where to knock.

subtitle: The command that lets two servers exchange data without forcing the user to wait.

tldr.problem: When a user wants to copy a file from one server to another, both servers must coordinate to open a data connection, but neither knows when the other will be ready.
tldr.mechanism: The PASV command tells a server to listen for an incoming connection instead of initiating one. A user can send PASV to one server and a transfer command to another, and they connect directly.
tldr.outcome: This became the standard way for FTP servers to negotiate third-party transfers, still used today in FTP clients and as the basis for passive mode in SFTP.

today: The PASV command became the foundation of passive mode FTP, widely used by clients today to avoid firewall issues. It is also the basis for passive mode in SFTP.

sections.title: The Third-Party Transfer Problem
sections.content:
In FTP, a user normally connects to a server, commands it, and receives data. But sometimes a user wants to copy a file from one server (B) to another (C) directly. Both servers must coordinate without the user in the middle.

The challenge is that without prior agreement, one server might try to connect while the other is not ready, or both might try to connect at the same time. This RFC, following discussion at an FTP meeting at BBN in March 1973, proposes the PASV command to solve this.
sections.eli5: Two servers need to talk to each other, but they do not know when the other is ready. A signal tells one server to wait by the phone while the other server calls.

sections.title: PASV and SOCK Commands
sections.content:
Two commands work together for third-party transfers. The SOCK command tells a server which socket to use and which host to expect a connection from. The PASV command tells a server to open its data socket for listening and wait for an incoming connection.

When a server receives PASV, it acknowledges positively, confirming that its data socket is open and listening. When an incoming connection arrives at that socket, the server responds with a matching connection to complete the data path.
sections.eli5: SOCK is like writing down an address. PASV is like saying 'wait here.' The server that got PASV sits at the door, and when the other server arrives, they connect directly.

sections.title: A Data Transfer Scenario
sections.content:
The user first tells server B about the location (SOCK) of server C, and server C about the location of server B. Then the user sends PASV to server B, making it listen on its data socket. Finally, the user can send transfer commands in any order: STOR (store) to server B and RTRV (retrieve) to server C. The servers connect to each other and exchange data without further user involvement.

This design lets both servers understand the transfer parameters before connecting. For security, sending a SOCK command to the same host that will receive PASV allows the receiving server to verify the incoming connection is expected.
sections.eli5: First, tell both servers about each other. Then tell one to wait. Then tell both to start. They find each other and swap the file.
